source.title: Investigating the Impact of Quantization Methods on the Safety and Reliability of Large Language Models
source.authors: Artem Kharinaev; Viktor Moskvoretskii; Egor Shvetsov; Kseniia Studenikina; Mikhail Bykov; E. Burnaev

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some table formatting is flattened or irregular, but the document is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether model safety changes under weight quantization, a different model-compression setting from the claim’s fine-tuning, token-position, and safety-localization versions.
record.gate_note: Reports open-ended unsafe/safe response outcomes under quantization. These findings concern safety behavior but do not test the specific interventions or mechanisms named in V1–V7. SafetyBench multiple-choice results measure safety-concept accuracy, not refusal or harmful-completion rates, so they are not included as rows for these versions. The paper also cites findings from other work; those cited results are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study measures how post-training quantization and quantization-aware training change open-ended safety ratios. It has no harmful or benign fine-tuning manipulation (V1/V2), no per-token KL (V3), no prefill, suffix or decoding attack (V4), no localization analysis (V5/V6) and no deepening method (V7). It cites Qi et al. 2023 only to argue that alignment is fragile. The QAT runs (STE, QLoRA) involve training, but the training data and objective are not described, and quantization is confounded with the training. They therefore cannot stand as a test of V2. The record's 'tests' relation contradicts its own finding that no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress three further points. Multiple-choice safety benchmarks (SafetyBench) fail to detect the degradation, sometimes ranking quantized models as safe as FP16 or safer. QAT models are less safe than the abliterated Llama. OpenSafetyMini exposes quantization-induced safety drops better than XSafety.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates post-training quantization and quantization-aware training; it does not reproduce fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples, token-position KL measurement, or token-prefill bypass tests.
record.method_sensitivity: Safety outcomes vary across quantization method, precision, model, and benchmark; the paper also reports that multiple-choice evaluation can disagree with open-ended safety evaluation.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight quantization lowers open-ended safety ratios, depending on method, precision, model size and benchmark. Examples: Llama QUIP# int2 drops from 93.06 to 84.25, and Mistral QUIP# int2 from 84.82 to 70.10 on OpenSafetyMini. QUIK int4 and AQLM int2 largely preserve safety.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-training weight quantization can erode safety behaviour, with the size of the loss depending on quantizer and bit width.

fits_no_version.finding: Quantization-aware training (STE, QLoRA) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct cuts the OpenSafetyMini safety ratio from 93.06 to 13–45%. This is worse than the abliterated model (63.26 by LLM judge, 58.67% safe by humans).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quantization-aware training that optimizes task loss without alignment data can largely remove safety behaviour.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the safety ratios. The paper reports interrater agreement (Krippendorff’s α = 0.623) and 92% agreement between the LLM judge and human judgments, but those do not provide uncertainty intervals for the reported model outcomes. Table 9 has an irregular flattened entry for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct at int2, and this record does not use its ambiguous XSafety value.
record.rows_left_out: Three safety-ratio results omitted to remain under the 60-row limit: Table 9, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct QUIP# int2 on XSafety (ambiguous flattened layout); Table 10, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct STE int4 on XSafety; and Table 10, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct STE int3 on XSafety. The corresponding OpenSafetyMini QAT conditions and the other PTQ safety results are retained.

untested.parts: No benign fine-tuning with described data. QAT training data and objective are unspecified and confounded with quantization.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding-change attacks.
No localization of safety in weights. The abliterated checkpoint is only evaluated, not analysed. QUIK's salient-vector explanation is speculative.
No test of what causes shallowness.

record.verdict_notes: The study is about quantization, not fine-tuning. The only link to the phenomenon is its speculative discussion that SFT/RLHF-introduced alignment is fragile, citing Qi et al. 2023. Abliterated-model LLM-judge values (XSafety 83.32, OpenSafetyMini 63.26) are not recorded as rows, but they bear on no version. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or harmful-request compliance after such fine-tuning.
No benign-data fine-tuning or its effect on harmful compliance.
No per-token KL measurement or comparison of response positions.
No prefilling, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change bypass test.
No test that a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior. The abliterated checkpoint is evaluated, but the study does not perform or analyze its refusal-direction removal.
No test of whether training data or objective produces shallow safety.
No training to deepen safety across response tokens or evaluation of whether such deepening holds up.
